(CNN) -- Watch out! Lock up your loved ones! Another bloated, over-produced, high-concept monstrosity has escaped from the labs at Dreamworks Animation, and it's out to devour your kids. Susan, aka "Ginormica," has to save the world in "Monsters vs. Aliens." But don't be too alarmed. "Monsters vs. Aliens" is relatively harmless -- a toothless satire with a knee-jerk feminist theme and a sorry excuse for a plot. That sounds harsh, I know. Who doesn't want to see a 50-foot woman careening through San Francisco on skates that turn out to be automobiles -- the ultimate demolition roller derby? But think about that, just for a second. Roller skates work because they have fixed wheels. Try it with motorcars and you won't get very far. Is that too picky? Perhaps, but you wouldn't find Pixar playing so fast and loose with the laws of physics, and that kind of inattention to detail is typical of the lackadaisical storytelling here and in other Dreamworks animated features. (The talent pool for this one includes the directors of "Shrek 2" and "Shark Tale" and the writers of "Kung Fu Panda" and "The Rocker," incidentally.) High concepts, top-notch voice talent and scattershot pop cultural references are no compensation for a coherent script. The XXXL lady in question -- dubbed "Ginormica" by her U.S. military guards -- starts out plain and petite Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), until a meteorite hits her just minutes before she's supposed to tie the knot with unctuous chauvinist Derek (Paul Rudd). Her rapid growth spurt saves her from that particular fate worse than death, even if at first glance her new roommates don't look like much of an improvement. There's Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist who semi-advertently mutated with a bug; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen) an amorphous blue jelly-like blob who gets on just fine without a brain; Missing Link (Will Arnett), a gung-ho amphibian who's all mouth; and a giant dust mite called Insectosaurus who isn't voiced by anyone because he doesn't have anything to say. Sci-fi fans will have fun counting off the references to myriad classics -- "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Invaders from Mars," "The Fly," "The Creature from the Black Lagoon," "The Blob," "Mothra" and "Attack of the 50-Foot Woman," for starters -- and noting a few clever bits and pieces (Kiefer Sutherland, as General W.R. Monger, riffs on George C. Scott in "Dr. Strangelove"). The trouble is, once the introductions are over, the filmmakers can only launch their desperately limp plot: The White House turns to these monstrous superheroes to save the planet from evil Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson), a squidlike creature with four eyes and twice as many legs, and a one-eyed tin robot to do his dirty work for him. Ginormica gets a kick-butt finale, and is a much stronger character -- in any number of ways -- than the movie's president. (In a genuinely witty casting touch he's voiced by Stephen Colbert.) That may be good politics or at least a sound marketing decision from the studio's perspective -- it's been awhile since a family animated feature produced a genuinely strong female character (unless you count "Coraline," which was way too scary for my family) -- but Susan's self-esteem is an awfully long time coming. iReport.com: What do you think of 'Monsters vs. Aliens'? (Bizarrely -- and maybe it's just my imagination -- Gallaxhar bears a passing resemblance to President Obama. I wonder ... would that make Susan/Ginormica a surrogate for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?) Visually, too, "Monsters vs Aliens" is undistinguished, although its shortcomings may be disguised if you seek out the 3-D version. Funny how 3-D movies tend to produce two-dimensional characters, with "Coraline" again the exception to the rule. Jocular and unpretentiously trashy, "Monsters vs. Aliens" should be a lot of fun -- and it is, in places. But the truth is it's as hung up on itself as Susan's preening fiance. Hand on heart, I had a better time at "Space Chimps." "Monsters vs. Aliens" runs 94 minutes and is rated PG. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

# A Review of "Monsters vs. Aliens"

"Monsters vs. Aliens" stands as a prime example of everything that can go wrong when spectacle takes precedence over substance. Rather than delivering a satisfying cinematic experience, the film emerges as an over-produced, high-concept exercise that ultimately collapses under the weight of its own ambitions. It lacks both a coherent plot and the kind of meaningful satire that might have justified its existence, leaving audiences with little more than a hollow display of animated excess.

Nowhere is the film's carelessness more apparent than in its blithe disregard for the laws of physics. In one particularly egregious moment, a pair of roller skates somehow function as fully capable automobiles—a detail that captures the lackadaisical storytelling that has become all too characteristic of Dreamworks animated features. Such moments betray a fundamental indifference to internal logic, as though the filmmakers assumed that dazzling visuals could paper over the cracks in their narrative foundation.

This is precisely where Dreamworks reveals its shortcomings when measured against its chief rival, Pixar. Where Pixar consistently demonstrates a meticulous attention to detail and a genuine respect for storytelling craft, Dreamworks seems content to lean on the crutches of star-studded voice casts and a steady stream of pop culture references. Unfortunately, no amount of celebrity talent or topical humor can compensate for a script that is fundamentally weak at its core.

The plot itself follows Susan Murphy, a young woman whose life takes a dramatic turn when she is struck by a meteorite on the very day of her wedding. The impact transforms her into a fifty-foot giant, earning her the name "Ginormica" and derailing her impending marriage to a fiancé whose self-centered nature makes him an unworthy partner in any case. From there, Susan finds herself thrust into a strange new world populated by fellow monsters.

Her companions form a motley ensemble, each drawn from the tradition of classic monster movies. Among them are a mad scientist, a brainless blob, an amphibious creature, and a giant dust mite. While this cast of characters offers occasional moments of amusement, they are ultimately unable to elevate the film beyond its fundamental flaws.

# Monsters vs. Aliens: A Review

DreamWorks Animation's "Monsters vs. Aliens" is a high-concept CGI feature that promises much and delivers little. At its center is Susan Murphy, an ordinary young woman whose wedding day takes a catastrophic turn when she's struck by a falling meteorite and transformed into a 50-foot giant. Rechristened "Ginormica" and voiced by Reese Witherspoon, Susan is whisked away by a secret government agency and thrown together with a ragtag band of misfit monsters. It's a setup ripe with comedic and imaginative potential, and one that gestures affectionately toward the creature features of the 1950s.

Unfortunately, the film squanders that potential at nearly every turn. What should have been a sharp, loving satire of classic monster movies instead emerges as toothless and incoherent, unwilling to commit to any coherent comic vision. The jokes land with a shrug rather than a punch, and the parody never develops enough bite to satisfy either nostalgic adults or curious children.

The storytelling proves especially frustrating on the level of basic plot logic. The film plays fast and loose with its own rules, particularly when it comes to physics. Susan's size seems to fluctuate according to the demands of any given scene rather than any consistent internal logic, and the narrative repeatedly asks viewers to overlook gaps and contrivances that a tighter script would have resolved. The result is a movie that feels assembled rather than written—a collection of set pieces in search of a story.

In place of genuine wit and structural coherence, the filmmakers lean heavily on the crutches that have become DreamWorks trademarks: a roster of recognizable celebrity voices and a steady stream of pop-culture references. These elements offer momentary flashes of recognition but no lasting substance. They substitute for the careful craftsmanship that distinguishes the best animated features, papering over a fundamentally underdeveloped screenplay with surface-level flash.

Ultimately, "Monsters vs. Aliens" underscores the persistent gap between DreamWorks and its chief rival, Pixar. Where Pixar's films are built on emotional truth, narrative discipline, and a deep respect for storytelling, DreamWorks too often settles for a more lackadaisical approach—content to dazzle the eye while neglecting the heart and mind. For all its impressive animation and clever premise, "Monsters vs. Aliens" is a reminder that spectacle alone cannot compensate for a story that never fully takes shape.

# 'Monsters vs. Aliens': DreamWorks Aims High but Falls Short of Pixar's Magic

**By CNN Film Critic**

There's a moment about halfway through DreamWorks Animation's "Monsters vs. Aliens" when you realize you've been watching a lot of frenetic action without feeling much of anything. It's a familiar sensation for anyone who has followed the studio's output over the years—technically impressive, occasionally funny, but curiously hollow at its core.

## A Premise Full of Promise

The setup has plenty of B-movie charm. Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon) gets struck by a meteor on her wedding day and grows into a 50-foot giant. Captured by the government, she's renamed Ginormica and drafted into a ragtag team of monsters to defend Earth from an alien invasion led by the tentacled Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson).

The monster crew—including the brainy blob B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), the fish-ape hybrid Missing Link (Will Arnett), and the mad scientist Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie)—offers loving nods to 1950s creature features. It's the kind of concept that should soar.

## Style Over Substance

And there lies the problem. Where Pixar builds films around emotional truth—think of the opening montage of "Up" or the existential ache of "WALL-E"—"Monsters vs. Aliens" settles for spectacle. The 3-D effects are undeniably slick, with objects hurtling toward the audience at every opportunity, but the gimmickry can't disguise a screenplay that never digs beneath its surface.

Susan's arc toward self-empowerment feels sketched rather than earned. We're told she's finding her strength, but the film is too busy racing to its next set piece to let the sentiment land. Compare this to how Pixar patiently develops its characters, and the gap in ambition becomes painfully clear.

## Laughs That Don't Quite Connect

The voice cast works hard, and Seth Rogen gets some genuine laughs as the good-natured, brainless B.O.B. But too many jokes rely on pop-culture references that feel calculated to please parents rather than serve the story. It's the DreamWorks formula—wink at the adults, dazzle the kids—and it's starting to feel awfully tired.

## The Verdict

"Monsters vs. Aliens" isn't a bad film. Young children will likely be entertained, and the visual craftsmanship is genuine. But entertainment and artistry aren't the same thing. Pixar has spent a decade proving that animated films can move us as deeply as any live-action drama. By that standard, DreamWorks' latest feels content merely to keep us distracted.

It's colorful, it's loud, and it's forgettable—the cinematic equivalent of cotton candy. Enjoy it in the moment, but don't expect it to nourish.

**Rating: 2.5 out of 4 stars**

# "Monsters vs. Aliens": A Cosmic Collision of Recycled Ideas That Somehow Works

**⭐⭐⭐ out of 5 stars**

Ah, DreamWorks. The animation studio that looked at Pixar's emotional storytelling and said, "What if we just threw pop culture references at a wall and animated the splatter?" Their 2009 offering, *Monsters vs. Aliens*, is exactly what it sounds like—a film title generated by a committee of executives who fell asleep during a B-movie marathon.

## The "Plot," Such As It Is

Our heroine Susan Murphy gets bonked by a meteor on her wedding day (because nothing says comedy like ruining a woman's life), grows to fifty feet tall, and gets rebranded "Ginormica." She's promptly kidnapped by the government—thanks, freedom—and tossed into a monster prison. Revolutionary stuff, truly.

## The Cast: A Star-Studded Cry for Help

**Reese Witherspoon** lends her plucky voice to Susan, doing her level best to inject pathos into a movie about a gelatinous blob. Speaking of which, **Seth Rogen** voices B.O.B., the brainless blue goo, essentially playing himself but with fewer brain cells and, remarkably, more coherent life choices.

**Hugh Laurie** slums it as Dr. Cockroach, Ph.D. (the Ph.D. is very important), while **Will Arnett** growls through The Missing Link. **Rainn Wilson** hams up villain duties as the tentacled Gallaxhar, delivering the film's only genuinely entertaining performance—a four-eyed megalomaniac with abandonment issues and cloning problems.

## The Sci-Fi "Homages" (Read: Theft)

The film wears its influences like a stolen letterman jacket. There's the *Attack of the 50 Ft. Woman* premise, the *Close Encounters* five-note musical exchange (which they actually pull off with surprising charm), *The Blob*, *The Fly*, and roughly seventeen thousand nods to 1950s creature features. It's less a movie than a Wikipedia article on retro sci-fi, animated in glorious 3D—because 2009 legally required everything to poke you in the eye.

## The Verdict

Here's the infuriating part: **it's actually kind of fun.** For all my complaining, the alien invasion set-pieces have zip, Wilson's villain is a delight, and there's a shockingly sweet message about self-acceptance buried under the explosions.

It's not *WALL-E*. It's not trying to be. It's a loud, colorful, aggressively adequate popcorn flick that'll entertain your kids and mildly amuse you while you check your phone.

**Bottom line:** Monsters win. Aliens lose. Your brain takes a well-deserved nap.

# Monsters vs. Aliens: DreamWorks' Spectacle Over Substance

There's a moment early in DreamWorks Animation's *Monsters vs. Aliens* when our heroine, Susan Murphy, is struck by a meteor on her wedding day and swells to a towering fifty feet. It's a genuinely arresting image—the bride in white ballooning past the church steeple—and for a fleeting instant, you sense the film this could have been: a witty, heartfelt riff on transformation and self-acceptance dressed in monster-movie clothing. Then the plot machinery grinds into gear, the pop-culture references start flying, and *Monsters vs. Aliens* settles comfortably into the middle of the road, where DreamWorks has pitched its tent for the better part of a decade.

Released in the same season that gave us the aching beauty of *Coraline* and following on the heels of Pixar's near-perfect *WALL-E*, the film arrives at an awkward moment for its studio. The animation landscape has shifted beneath DreamWorks' feet, and *Monsters vs. Aliens* feels like a movie unaware that the bar has been raised—or perhaps aware and simply uninterested in clearing it.

To be fair, the picture looks handsome enough. Directors Rob Letterman and Conrad Vernon clearly relish the exaggerated scale of their premise, and the 3D presentation—much touted at the time of release—occasionally justifies the ticket surcharge with a paddle-ball to the face here, a plummeting satellite there. But spectacle without soul is a hollow thing, and here is where the comparison to its contemporaries becomes unkind but unavoidable. Where Pixar constructs its films around a bruising emotional truth—loneliness, mortality, the terror of being forgotten—DreamWorks constructs its films around a marketable concept and trusts a game voice cast to paper over the gaps.

And what a cast it is, ostensibly. Reese Witherspoon lends Susan a pleasant, plucky earnestness, but the script gives her precious little to work with beyond a rote empowerment arc that resolves with all the surprise of a sunrise. Susan is meant to be the beating heart of the ensemble, yet she remains curiously inert, a protagonist defined more by her dimensions than her desires. Witherspoon does what she can, but you can't animate a character out of thin material, no matter how bright the voice.

The supporting monsters fare a bit better, largely because they're allowed to be broad. Hugh Laurie brings a fussy, professorial dignity to Dr. Cockroach, and Will Arnett's The Missing Link is a serviceable washed-up jock, all bluster and swagger. Seth Rogen, voicing the gelatinous B.O.B., delivers exactly the affable stoner shtick you'd expect—amusing in ten-second bursts, wearying across ninety minutes. There's a laugh or two in his cheerful brainlessness, but the joke never deepens; it simply repeats, louder. Rainn Wilson chews the scenery with evident glee as the squid-like alien villain Gallaxhar, and Kiefer Sutherland barks military clichés as General W.R. Monger with a gravelly commitment the material scarcely deserves. Stephen Colbert turns up as a bumbling U.S. President, mugging through a set-piece involving an alien probe and a Beverly Hills Cop keyboard riff that lands as the film's most self-satisfied gag.

Here's the problem: these are talented, funny people, and yet the whole enterprise feels less like a story than a delivery system for their individual bits. *Monsters vs. Aliens* is assembled rather than composed. Each character has a designated function, each set-piece its designated payoff, and the connective tissue between them is a slurry of references to 1950s creature features that younger audiences won't recognize and older ones will find merely cute rather than clever. The film wants credit for its affection toward the B-movies it plunders, but affection is not the same as invention. Homage, absent a fresh idea of its own, is just nostalgia wearing a costume.

Consider, by contrast, what Henry Selick accomplished with *Coraline* earlier that same year. That film understood that children can handle genuine unease, that beauty and menace can coexist, that a story for young audiences need not talk down to them or drown them in noise. Its stop-motion craft was painstaking, tactile, alive with a handmade strangeness. *Monsters vs. Aliens*, by comparison, feels frictionless and disposable—competent pixels arranged in pleasing patterns, engineered to sell toys and move popcorn, gone from memory before you've reached the parking lot.

The deeper frustration is that the premise had real promise. A movie about literal monsters embraced as heroes, about the outcasts saving the very society that imprisoned them—there's thematic meat on those bones. But the screenplay, credited to a committee of no fewer than five writers, never trusts its own metaphor. It gestures toward ideas about belonging and being underestimated, then hurries past them toward the next explosion, terrified that a quiet moment might cost it the room. Pixar built *WALL-E* around forty near-wordless minutes of pure visual storytelling. DreamWorks can't abide five seconds of silence.

None of this makes *Monsters vs. Aliens* a disaster. It's brisk, colorful, and intermittently funny, and small children will likely be diverted by the bright chaos of it all. But "diverted" is a low ceiling, and in a year when animation reached for the sublime, mere diversion feels like a missed opportunity dressed up in 3D glasses. DreamWorks had the cast, the technology, and a premise brimming with possibility. What it lacked was the courage to make us feel something—and in animation's new golden age, that lack is no longer forgivable.

**Two stars out of five.**

# When Giant Women Attack: "Monsters vs. Aliens" Fights Aliens, Loses to Logic

There's an old rule in filmmaking: if you're going to riff on the classics, you'd better bring something new to the table besides a 50-foot punchline. DreamWorks' *Monsters vs. Aliens* arrives armed with affectionate nods to sci-fi's golden age and a color palette bright enough to sedate a toddler—but somewhere between the homages and the plot holes, the movie forgets to make a lick of sense.

## A Loving Tribute (to Movies You'd Rather Rewatch)

Let's give credit where it's due: the film wears its influences on its enormous sleeve. Susan Murphy's growth spurt is lifted wholesale from *Attack of the 50 Foot Woman*. We get a gelatinous blob straight out of *The Blob*, a fish-man cousin of *Creature from the Black Lagoon*, and a mad-scientist cockroach that's basically *The Fly* with better diction. The insectosaurus? Pure Toho kaiju cinema, minus the rubber suit charm.

It's a greatest-hits album performed by a competent cover band. You'll recognize every tune, but you'll leave humming none of them.

## Plot Holes Bigger Than the Heroine

Where to begin? Susan gets bombarded by a meteorite made of "quantonium"—a substance so scientifically rigorous it might as well be called Plot Fuel—and instantly grows to skyscraper height. Yet her wedding dress grows *with* her. Physics, meet whimsy. Whimsy, please stop taking calls.

Then there's the government's ultra-secret monster prison, apparently funded well enough to imprison creatures for decades but not well enough to, say, *tell anyone monsters exist* until an alien invasion makes them convenient. General W.R. Monger (get it?) deploys these captives as a last resort, which raises the question: why keep them locked up for 50 years if they were the plan all along?

And don't get me started on Gallaxhar's invasion strategy—cloning himself thousands of times to conquer a planet he ultimately blows up. The villain's scheme has all the internal consistency of a fever dream scribbled on a napkin.

## Feminism, Now in Family-Size Portions

The film desperately wants to be a girl-power parable. Susan spends the first act defined entirely by her fiancé Derek, a self-absorbed weatherman whose ego needs its own zip code. Once she embraces her monstrous new self, she dumps him, saves the world, and learns she "never needed a man."

Noble sentiment! Except the movie can't decide whether it's empowering Susan or just swapping one set of external validators for another—her worth still hinges on being *literally the biggest, most powerful person in the room*. The message lands somewhere between "believe in yourself" and "you're only worthwhile once you're irradiated into a superhero." It's liberation with an asterisk, feminism as a plot device rather than a lived idea.

## The Verdict

*Monsters vs. Aliens* is loud, colorful, and occasionally clever—a serviceable distraction for kids and a nostalgia scavenger hunt for parents. But it mistakes reference for wit and empowerment for character development. It borrows the skeletons of better films without giving them anything to say.

Like its heroine, the movie is enormous. Unlike her, it never quite figures out what to do with all that size.

**★★☆☆☆ — Two stars, both of them quantonium.**

# 'Monsters vs. Aliens' delivers big laughs, bigger creatures

**By CNN Entertainment**

**Rating:** PG (for sci-fi action, some crude humor and mild language)
**Runtime:** 94 minutes
**In theaters:** Now playing, available in 3-D

---

(CNN) -- In an era when animated features increasingly reach for emotional depth and Pixar-style poignancy, DreamWorks Animation makes a refreshingly unapologetic choice with "Monsters vs. Aliens": It just wants to have fun.

And for the most part, it succeeds.

The film opens on the wedding day of Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), an ordinary California weather girl whose big day is spectacularly interrupted when a meteorite strikes her and transforms her into a 50-foot giantess. Whisked away by the government to a secret facility, she's rechristened "Ginormica" and thrown in with a ragtag band of monsters kept under lock and key for decades.

## A monster ensemble

The creatures are the movie's beating heart. There's the gelatinous, brainless B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), whose cheerful stupidity delivers many of the film's biggest laughs. The Missing Link (Will Arnett) is an over-the-hill fish-man convinced he's still an athletic terror. Dr. Cockroach, Ph.D. (Hugh Laurie) brings mad-scientist flair, and the towering, silent Insectosaurus rounds out the crew.

If there's a standout, it's Rogen's B.O.B., a blue blob whose lack of a brain becomes a running gag that somehow never wears thin. Witherspoon, meanwhile, grounds the chaos with genuine warmth, giving Susan an arc about self-empowerment that -- while hardly subtle -- gives the film a spine.

Stealing scenes on the villain side is Rainn Wilson's Gallaxhar, a squid-like alien overlord whose cloning-obsessed monologues are a comic highlight. Kiefer Sutherland gruffly barks his way through the role of General W.R. Monger with obvious relish.

## Animation that pops -- especially in 3-D

Visually, "Monsters vs. Aliens" was engineered as a 3-D showcase, and it shows. Paddleballs, alien tentacles and falling debris all come hurtling toward the audience with gleeful abandon. The animation is bright, fluid and confidently designed, with a retro affection for 1950s creature features baked into every frame.

The set pieces -- a Golden Gate Bridge showdown chief among them -- are staged with genuine energy. This is a movie that understands scale and uses it.

## The verdict

Where "Monsters vs. Aliens" stumbles is in its ambition, or rather its lack of it. The story is thin, the emotional beats predictable, and the pop-culture references may date faster than the animation. It reaches for spectacle over substance, and viewers hoping for the layered storytelling of the genre's best may leave a little hungry.

But as a bright, loud, good-natured romp -- particularly for younger audiences and families -- it more than earns its runtime. Sometimes a movie about a giant woman punching an alien robot is exactly what a Saturday afternoon calls for.

**Bottom line:** Big, colorful and cheerfully silly, "Monsters vs. Aliens" won't change animation, but it'll keep the whole family grinning.
